title: Question 5
stem:
Two point sources, $A$ and $B$, produce coherent electromagnetic waves. The waves from $A$ and $B$ are emitted in phase and have wavelength $\lambda$, as shown in Fig. 5.1.

{{figure:figure_5_1}}

Fig. 5.1 (not to scale)

The lines on Fig. 5.1 represent wavefronts. All the points on a wavefront are in phase.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.part_stem: On Fig. 5.1, mark with a cross ($\times$):
parts.text: the position of an interference maximum (label this cross Y)

markscheme_points.text: cross labelled Y drawn: at any position where wavefronts cross or centrally in a ‘diamond’ shape formed between any adjacent wavefronts from A and B

hints: Hint 1: Think about what the curved lines mean - each line is a crest, so where do two crests meet to reinforce each other?
parts.proper_answer: Mark Y with a cross where a wavefront from A crosses a wavefront from B.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture What Maximum Means**
Think of each curved line as a crest of the wave. When a crest meets a crest, the displacements add up to give a large amplitude. That is constructive interference, which gives an interference maximum.

Step 2: **Spot It On The Diagram**
Since the two sources are in phase, constructive happens where the path difference is zero or a whole number of wavelengths. On the picture that is simply where the two sets of circles intersect. So place Y exactly on any crossing point of an A-wavefront and a B-wavefront.

parts.text: the position of an interference minimum (label this cross Z).

markscheme_points.text: cross labelled Z drawn on a wavefront from one source at a point midway between adjacent wavefronts from the other source

hints: Hint 1: Think about where cancellation happens - where a crest from one source falls exactly halfway between two crests from the other source.
parts.proper_answer: Mark Z with a cross on a wavefront from one source midway between two adjacent wavefronts from the other source.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture What Minimum Means**
A minimum is cancellation. A crest from A arrives at the same time as a trough from B, so they cancel to near zero. That needs a path difference of half a wavelength, $\lambda/2$, $3\lambda/2$, and so on.

Step 2: **Spot It On The Diagram**
Troughs lie halfway between the drawn crests. So look for a place where a solid line from A sits exactly in the gap between two solid lines from B, or vice versa. Place Z there, on one wavefront and centrally between the two from the other source.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
The waves in air have a wavelength of $2.9 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m}$.

An interference pattern is detected along a line parallel to $AB$ and at a perpendicular distance of $140 \text{ m}$ from $AB$. The spacing between adjacent interference maxima is $1.2 \text{ cm}$.
parts.text: Calculate the separation $a$ of the sources $A$ and $B$.
hints: Hint 1: Focus on the fringe pattern far away - the spacing $x$ of bright fringes is linked to wavelength $\lambda$, source separation $a$ and screen distance $D$.
Hint 2: Rearrange that link to make the source separation $a$ the subject, and convert the 1.2 cm fringe spacing into metres before substituting.
Hint 3: Substitute $\lambda = 2.9 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m}$, $D = 140 \text{ m}$ and $x = 1.2 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$ and evaluate to 2 significant figures.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall The Fringe Formula**
For two coherent sources observed far away, the bright fringes are evenly spaced. The link is: $$\lambda = \frac{ax}{D}$$ where $\lambda$ is wavelength, $a$ is source separation, $x$ is spacing between adjacent maxima, and $D$ is perpendicular distance to the observation line.

Step 2: **Rearrange For a**
You need $a$, so multiply both sides by $D$ and divide by $x$: $$a = \frac{\lambda D}{x}$$ Check units: $x = 1.2 \text{ cm} = 1.2 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$, $D = 140 \text{ m}$, $\lambda = 2.9 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m}$.

Step 3: **Substitute And Calculate**
$$a = \frac{(2.9 \times 10^{-5}) \times 140}{1.2 \times 10^{-2}}$$ $$a \approx 0.338 \text{ m} \approx 0.34 \text{ m}$$ That is a sensible laboratory-scale separation for such a wide fringe pattern with a long wavelength.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: State the principal region of the electromagnetic spectrum to which the waves belong.
hints: Hint 1: Convert the wavelength to micrometres and recall where visible light sits - about 0.4 to 0.7 micrometres - so is this longer or shorter than red light?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Place The Wavelength On The Spectrum**
$$\lambda = 2.9 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m} = 29 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$$ Visible light is roughly $4 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$ to $7 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$. This wave is about 40 times longer than red light, but much shorter than microwaves and radio waves. That region just beyond red is the infrared region.
